title: Heme metabolism
covers: How heme is built in eight steps from glycine and succinyl CoA, how ALA synthase is regulated, acute intermittent porphyria versus lead poisoning, and how heme is broken down to bilirubin, conjugated and excreted, with Gilbert syndrome as the case.

summary.h: Heme and where it is made

ul: Heme (Fe-protoporphyrin IX) is the prosthetic group of hemoglobin, myoglobin, mitochondrial and microsomal cytochromes, catalase, peroxidases and tryptophan pyrrolase.

Structure: four pyrrole rings joined by methine bridges (–CH=) form the porphyrin ring, with iron at the center. Eight side chains, two per pyrrole: methyl, vinyl or propionate, in the order MVMVMPPM.
All aerobic cells are presumed able to make heme.

table: Erythroid cells of the bone marrow

ul: Glycine + succinyl CoA, eight reactions. The first and the last three are mitochondrial; the steps in between are cytoplasmic. Heme feeds back negatively on the first enzyme.

items.caption: The eight steps of heme synthesis

table: Hydroxymethylbilane: four PBG head to tail, a linear tetrapyrrole
Uroporphyrinogen III: rearranged and cyclized, octacarboxylate
Coproporphyrinogen III: the four acetate groups lose their carboxyls, tetracarboxylate
Protoporphyrinogen IX: two propionates become vinyls, dicarboxylate
Protoporphyrin IX: six hydrogens removed, the first porphyrin (oxidized)

ul: Without URO-synthase, HMB cyclizes nonenzymatically to uroporphyrinogen I.
Everything before protoporphyrin IX is a porphyrinogen (reduced form).
ALA synthase is rate-limiting and therefore highly regulated. Two isoforms:

table: Repressed by the free heme pool. Induced by fasting and by cytochrome P450-inducing drugs, which use up heme. Repressed by glucose
Erythropoietin and iron: translation stops when iron is low

ul: Defects in ALAS2 cause X-linked sideroblastic anemia.
If a downstream enzyme is partly blocked, heme falls, feedback is lost, ALAS1 is induced and ALA and PBG are overproduced. This is the basis of the acute attack.
Rare disorders, each a deficiency of one heme synthesis enzyme. Usually autosomal dominant or recessive, sometimes sporadic. They show up where the pathway is busiest: bone marrow and liver.
A block causes accumulation of precursors and lack of product, and both can be toxic.

items.note: Only acute intermittent porphyria needs to be known by name; the other porphyria names on the slides are marked FYI.

items.p: A 26-year-old woman has 3 days of severe abdominal pain with vomiting and constipation, a soft abdomen and a normal CT. She began a strict low-calorie diet two weeks ago and a sulfonamide five days ago. Pulse 118, BP 150/95, sodium 126, confusion, weak arms, and urine that turns reddish-brown on standing.

ul: Why now: the sulfonamide induces P450s and fasting induces ALAS1, so the liver is asked for more heme and more ALA enters the pathway.

Urine: ALA high, PBG markedly high, because ALA dehydratase still works and PBG piles up in front of the half-working enzyme. PBG oxidizes on standing to a reddish-brown pigment. No blisters, because the block comes before any porphyrin.
Diagnosis: HMB synthase (PBG deaminase) deficiency, autosomal dominant. Activity is halved and most carriers never have an attack.

table: Drugs that drive ALAS1 (sulfonamides …), fasting, progesterone, alcohol
Abdominal pain, tachycardia, hypertension, neuropathy, confusion, low sodium; no skin signs
Often taken for an acute abdomen or a psychiatric illness; some patients have unnecessary surgery
Stop the trigger, IV glucose, IV hemin (restores heme feedback on ALAS1), then avoid unsafe drugs

ul: Lead strongly inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase. ALA rises in the blood without a rise in PBG.

table: Inherited HMB synthase at half activity
Acquired: lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase
Yes: heme synthesis in red cell precursors is blocked

ul: Urine PBG is the test that separates them.

items.note: Clinical Sciences (microcytic anemia, slide 32) lists ALA synthase as inhibited by lead. This lecture names ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, which matches standard sources.

ul: Red cells live 120 days. The spleen acts as a sieve for red cell quality; old cells release hemoglobin, which is split into heme and globin.
The porphyrin ring is hydrophobic and must be made soluble to be excreted. This happens in macrophages of the reticulo-endothelial system, mostly in the spleen.

table: Opens the ring; releases Fe²⁺ and CO
Uses NADPH; gives the yellow-red pigment

ul: Bilirubin is a cellular antioxidant: a mildly high level without liver disease may be beneficial.
In hepatocytes, bilirubin UDP-glucuronyltransferase (UGT) adds glucuronic acid, giving bilirubin diglucuronide.
Conjugation makes bilirubin hydrophilic, so it travels in bile without a protein carrier. Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin is not normally secreted.
Conjugated (direct) bilirubin is actively transported into the bile canaliculi and on to the intestine.
In the gut, bacteria remove the glucuronic acid, and bilirubin becomes urobilinogen, mainly in the colon.

items.caption: The journey of bilirubin from the macrophage to feces and urine

ul: Hyperbilirubinemia gives jaundice: yellow tissues and sclerae. It usually signals liver disease (hepatocellular), obstruction or hemolytic anemia.
Too much unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood-brain barrier and deposit in the brain: kernicterus.
Labs measure total and direct bilirubin with reactive dyes; indirect bilirubin is calculated as total minus direct. Total bilirubin is normal up to 1.2 mg/dL.

items.p: A 21-year-old student fasting for Ramadan in exam week notices yellow eyes. He feels well, and urine and stools look normal. His eyes turned yellow once before, during a viral illness.

table: Total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL, almost all unconjugated
Bilirubin reaches the liver but leaves it unconjugated
Normal ALT, AST and alkaline phosphatase
Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and stays out of the urine
Rises with fasting or illness, normal when eating

ul: UGT1A1 works at about 30% of normal. Affects about 5–10% of people. Mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, worse with fasting, illness and stress.
Benign: no liver damage, no treatment, only reassurance.

cards.a: The first and the last three; the steps in between are cytoplasmic
Erythroid marrow cells (about 300 mg/day, for hemoglobin) and the liver (microsomal cytochromes)

cards.a: Methine bridges (–CH=)
ALA synthase; needs pyridoxal phosphate

URO-decarboxylase removes the carboxyls of the four acetate side chains: coproporphyrinogen III
COPRO-oxidase (mitochondria) turns two propionates into vinyls: protoporphyrinogen IX

ALA and PBG cause neurological signs; porphyrins and porphyrinogens cause skin photosensitivity

cards.a: Lead blocks heme synthesis in red cell precursors; half of HMB synthase activity is enough
Macrophages of the reticulo-endothelial system, mostly in the spleen

cards.a: Bacteria deconjugate it and form urobilinogen, mainly in the colon
Stercobilin (bacterial oxidation) colors feces; urobilin (kidney) colors urine
Unconjugated bilirubin crossing the blood-brain barrier into the brain
Calculated: total minus direct
UGT1A1 at about 30% of normal; 5–10% of people; mild unconjugated rise with fasting, illness, stress; reassurance only

cards.a: Normal hemoglobin, reticulocyte count and LDH

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has severe abdominal pain with a normal CT scan, a pulse of 118/min and a sodium of 126 mmol/L. She started a sulfonamide five days ago, and her urine darkens on standing. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: A neurovisceral attack with hyponatremia and dark urine after a P450-inducing drug is acute intermittent porphyria: HMB synthase (PBG deaminase) works at half activity. A: A block here would keep PBG from rising. C: Lead inhibits it; a block here builds up a porphyrin, not PBG. D: A block here builds up porphyrinogens, which cause skin signs. E: A heme degradation enzyme.

questions.stem: Two weeks into a strict low-calorie diet, a woman with a half-active heme synthesis enzyme has her first attack of abdominal pain. How does fasting set off the attack?

options.C: It depletes pyridoxal phosphate in the liver
options.D: It enlarges the hepatic free heme pool
options.E: It blocks iron entry into mitochondria

questions.explanation: Fasting induces ALAS1 (glucose represses it); more ALA then floods a pathway whose HMB synthase works at half capacity, and ALA and PBG pile up. B: Fasting acts on the first enzyme. C: Not the mechanism. D: Free heme represses ALAS1. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A sulfonamide precipitates an acute attack in a carrier of a heme synthesis defect. What is the first event in the liver?

options.B: The drug displaces heme from hemoglobin
options.C: The drug speeds glucose uptake into hepatocytes
options.D: The drug removes the cofactor of ALA synthase
options.E: Induced cytochrome P450s use up free heme

questions.explanation: Cytochrome P450-inducing drugs such as sulfonamides need heme: the free heme pool falls and ALAS1 is derepressed. A: Lead does that. B: Not the mechanism. C: Glucose represses ALAS1. D: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A woman with known acute intermittent porphyria is admitted after two days of vomiting and eating nothing. Which infusion directly represses her hepatic ALA synthase?
questions.explanation: Fasting induces ALAS1 and glucose represses it, so IV glucose is part of AIP treatment. A: The ALA synthase cofactor. B: Iron is not the treatment. D: Unrelated to heme synthesis. E: Not described as repressing ALAS1.

questions.stem: A woman with an inherited half-active HMB synthase has an attack after starting a sulfonamide. Which urinary compound is most markedly raised?
questions.explanation: In AIP urine ALA is high and PBG markedly high: ALA dehydratase keeps converting the extra ALA into PBG, which then piles up in front of HMB synthase. A: Lies beyond the block. B: Lies beyond the block. C: A heme breakdown product. E: A normal urine pigment.

questions.stem: A woman's fresh urine is pale yellow but turns reddish-brown after standing on the windowsill during an attack of abdominal pain and confusion. What explains the color change?
questions.explanation: On standing, PBG oxidizes to a reddish-brown pigment: that is why the urine darkens in an attack of acute intermittent porphyria. B: Stercobilin colors feces. C: She has no hemolysis. D: Not part of the attack. E: Not the cause here.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman in an acute porphyric attack has a markedly raised urine PBG but no blisters or sun sensitivity. Why is her skin spared?

options.A: Her porphyrins are cleared in bile
options.C: Skin damage needs a very high ALA level
options.D: The block lies before any porphyrin forms

questions.explanation: Only the precursors ALA and PBG (neurotoxic) accumulate; the block comes before the porphyrins, which cause photosensitivity. A: Porphyrins are not accumulating. B: Untreated patients also lack skin signs. C: ALA and PBG cause neurological signs. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A patient with an inherited defect of heme synthesis has neuropathy and confusion but normal skin. Which compounds are accumulating?
questions.explanation: Excess porphyrin precursors (ALA and PBG) are associated with neurological manifestations; excess porphyrins and porphyrinogens cause skin photosensitivity. A: Porphyrinogens cause skin photosensitivity. B: Porphyrinogens cause skin photosensitivity. C: A porphyrin; causes skin photosensitivity. D: Not a heme synthesis intermediate.

questions.stem: A patient with an inherited defect of heme synthesis has skin photosensitivity with blisters but no abdominal pain or neuropathy. Which intermediates are in excess?
questions.explanation: Each enzyme deficiency causes accumulation of intermediates: excess porphyrins/porphyrinogens cause skin photosensitivity, excess ALA and PBG neurological manifestations. A: A precursor; neurological effects. B: Precursors cause neurological effects. D: Heme breakdown products. E: Heme breakdown products.

questions.stem: A woman in an acute porphyric attack keeps vomiting despite IV glucose. Which drug restores heme feedback on hepatic ALA synthase?
questions.explanation: Treatment of an AIP attack: stop the trigger, IV glucose, and IV hemin, which restores heme feedback on ALAS1. A: Iron does not restore heme feedback. C: The ALA synthase cofactor. D: Unrelated to heme synthesis. E: Acts on erythroid cells.

questions.stem: Acute intermittent porphyria is autosomal dominant, yet a patient's father, who carries the same mutation, has never had an attack. What is the explanation?

options.A: His mutation lies in the erythroid isoform
options.B: Men cannot express the mutant HMB synthase
options.C: His bone marrow supplies heme to his liver
options.D: Half the enzyme activity is enough
options.E: He makes no ALA in the liver

questions.explanation: HMB synthase activity is halved and most carriers never have an attack: an attack needs a trigger that drives ALAS1. A: The defect is in HMB synthase, not ALA synthase. B: Not the explanation. C: Heme is made locally. E: He makes ALA normally.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has had two laparotomies for recurrent severe abdominal pain that found nothing. She now has confusion and a sodium of 124 mmol/L. Which condition was most likely missed?
questions.explanation: AIP is often misdiagnosed as an acute abdomen or a psychiatric illness, and some patients have unnecessary surgery. A: Mild jaundice without pain. B: An anemia without attacks. C: No pain attacks. D: Hemolysis without hyponatremia.

questions.stem: Each of the following can trigger an attack of acute intermittent porphyria EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: An attack needs a trigger that drives ALAS1: some drugs (sulfonamides), fasting, progesterone, alcohol. Glucose represses ALAS1. A: A listed trigger. B: A listed trigger. D: A listed trigger. E: A listed trigger.

questions.stem: A woman has severe abdominal pain with vomiting and a normal CT scan. Which additional finding would argue against an acute porphyric attack from HMB synthase deficiency?
questions.explanation: ALA and PBG are neurotoxic: abdominal pain, tachycardia, hypertension, neuropathy, confusion and low sodium, with no skin signs. A: Hypertension fits. C: Tachycardia fits. D: Low sodium fits. E: Neuropathy fits.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old living in an old house with peeling paint has abdominal pain and anemia. Urine ALA is high and urine PBG is normal. Inhibition of which enzyme explains the normal PBG?
questions.explanation: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase (and ferrochelatase): ALA rises in the absence of a rise in PBG. B: A block here would raise PBG. C: A block here would lower ALA. D: Acts beyond PBG. E: A heme degradation enzyme.

questions.stem: A man has abdominal pain and neuropathy, and urine ALA is high. Which urine test best separates acute intermittent porphyria from lead poisoning?
questions.explanation: Urine PBG is high in AIP and normal in lead poisoning (ALA dehydratase is inhibited). A: High in both. C: A heme breakdown product. D: A heme breakdown product. E: Not a porphyria marker.

questions.stem: Why does lead poisoning cause anemia while acute intermittent porphyria does not?

options.A: Lead causes chronic blood loss from the gut
options.B: Lead binds the oxygen site of hemoglobin
options.C: Lead blocks heme synthesis in red cell precursors

questions.explanation: Lead strongly blocks two enzymes in the very cells that make hemoglobin; in AIP half of the HMB synthase activity suffices for red cells. A: Not the mechanism. B: Not the mechanism. D: Not the mechanism. E: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase.

questions.stem: In lead poisoning, an acquired porphyria, protoporphyrin IX builds up in red cell precursors although iron is available. Which enzyme is inhibited?
questions.explanation: Ferrochelatase (heme synthetase) inserts ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX; with ALA dehydratase it is highly sensitive to heavy metals. A: Forms protoporphyrin IX. B: Acts two steps earlier. C: Acts in the cytoplasm. D: Acts in the cytoplasm.

questions.stem: A boy has a lifelong anemia, as did his maternal uncle. Both carry a defect in the erythroid-specific gene for the first enzyme of heme synthesis. Which gene is mutated?
questions.explanation: ALA synthase exists as a housekeeping form (ALAS1) and an erythroid-specific form (ALAS2); defects in ALAS2 cause X-linked sideroblastic anemia. A: The housekeeping isoform. B: Gilbert syndrome. C: AIP; no anemia. E: Not the first enzyme.

questions.stem: A defect in the erythroid-specific ALA synthase causes which disorder?
questions.explanation: Defects in ALAS2 cause X-linked sideroblastic anemia (XLSA). B: HMB synthase deficiency. C: Reduced UGT1A1. D: An enzyme defect of the hexose monophosphate shunt. E: Acquired, not genetic.

questions.stem: Severe vitamin B6 deficiency lowers pyridoxal phosphate in erythroblasts. Condensation of which substrates slows?
questions.explanation: ALA synthase condenses glycine and succinyl CoA into ALA using pyridoxal phosphate as a cofactor. A: Acetyl CoA is not used. B: Serine is not used. C: ALA dehydratase does this. D: HMB synthase.

questions.stem: Which step of heme synthesis is its main point of regulation?

options.A: Insertion of iron into protoporphyrin IX
options.B: Joining two ALA molecules into PBG
options.C: Condensation of glycine with succinyl CoA

questions.explanation: The first enzyme, ALA synthase, is rate-limiting and therefore highly regulated; heme exerts negative feedback on it. A: Ferrochelatase; not rate-limiting. B: ALA dehydratase; not rate-limiting. D: URO-synthase; not rate-limiting. E: Not rate-limiting.

questions.stem: What represses hepatic ALA synthase (ALAS1)?
questions.explanation: Liver ALAS1 is repressed by the hepatic "free heme" pool; P450-inducing drugs and fasting deplete heme and derepress it. B: Controls ALAS2. C: A substrate. D: Controls ALAS2 translation. E: A breakdown product.

questions.stem: A toddler with severe iron deficiency has erythroblasts short of iron. How is their ALA synthase (ALAS2), which is controlled by erythropoietin and iron, affected?

options.C: It is repressed by free heme

questions.explanation: Erythroid ALAS2 is controlled by erythropoietin and iron: translation stops when iron is low. A: That is the transferrin receptor response. C: That controls ALAS1. D: Fasting acts on ALAS1. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: In a liver with a partial block late in heme synthesis, heme output falls. Which change follows directly?
questions.explanation: A block downstream lowers heme, removes feedback and induces ALAS1, overproducing ALA and PBG: the basis of the acute attack. A: Not the consequence. B: A degradation enzyme. C: Not the consequence. E: Unrelated.

questions.stem: All cells with aerobic metabolism are presumed able to make heme. Which cells make the most heme per day?

options.A: Erythroid cells of the bone marrow
options.E: Macrophages of the red pulp in the spleen

questions.explanation: The first major site is the erythroid cells of the bone marrow (about 300 mg/day, mostly for hemoglobin); the second is the liver; adrenals and kidneys also make a sizable amount. B: The second major site. C: A sizable but smaller amount. D: A sizable but smaller amount. E: They break heme down.

questions.stem: Why does the liver need a steady supply of newly made heme?

options.A: Export of heme to developing red cells in marrow

questions.explanation: The liver is the second major site of heme synthesis because the rapid turnover of microsomal cytochromes requires newly formed heme. A: Erythroid cells make their own. B: Bilirubin comes from heme breakdown. C: Not the reason. D: Made in muscle.

questions.stem: Heme is a prosthetic group in each of the following proteins EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Heme functions as a prosthetic group for hemoglobin, myoglobin, mitochondrial and microsomal cytochromes, catalase, peroxidases and tryptophan pyrrolase. A: A heme protein. B: A heme protein. D: A heme protein. E: Heme proteins.

questions.stem: What links the four pyrrole rings of the porphyrin ring?
questions.explanation: Four pyrrole rings are joined by methine bridges (–CH=) to form the porphyrin ring. A: Join amino acids. C: Join cysteines. D: Side chains. E: Join sugars.

questions.stem: How many side chains substitute the porphyrin ring of heme?
questions.explanation: Eight side chains serve as substituents on the porphyrin ring, two on each pyrrole: propionate, methyl or vinyl, in the order MVMVMPPM. A: One per pyrrole is too few. B: Too few. C: Too many. E: Too many.

questions.stem: Which step of heme synthesis takes place in the cytoplasm?

options.A: Condensation of glycine and succinyl CoA

questions.explanation: The first reaction and the last three occur in mitochondria; ALA is transported to the cytoplasm, where ALA dehydratase condenses it into PBG. A: Mitochondrial. C: Mitochondrial. D: Mitochondrial. E: Mitochondrial.

questions.stem: Which reactions of the eight-step heme pathway occur in mitochondria?

options.A: The first and the last three
options.B: The first three and the last
options.C: The first two and the last two

questions.explanation: Heme is made from glycine and succinyl CoA in 8 reactions: the first and the last three occur in mitochondria, those in between in the cytoplasm. B: Reverses the pattern. C: Wrong split. D: Wrong split. E: Wrong split.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the entry of intermediates into mitochondria. After which product would heme synthesis stop?
questions.explanation: Coproporphyrinogen III, the last cytoplasmic product, enters the mitochondrion for the sixth step. A: Further cytoplasmic steps follow. B: Further cytoplasmic steps follow. D: One more cytoplasmic step follows. E: Formed inside mitochondria.

questions.stem: HMB synthase links four PBG molecules head to tail. What does it form?
questions.explanation: Hydroxymethylbilane synthase (PBG deaminase) catalyzes the head-to-tail condensation of four PBG molecules by deaminations into the linear tetrapyrrole hydroxymethylbilane. A: Cyclization is the next step. B: Protoporphyrinogen IX. C: Protoporphyrin IX. E: Four rings are joined.

questions.stem: What does uroporphyrinogen III synthase do to hydroxymethylbilane?

options.A: Removes four carboxyl groups from it
options.B: Removes six hydrogen atoms from it

questions.explanation: URO-synthase catalyzes the rearrangement and rapid cyclization of HMB into uroporphyrinogen III, the asymmetric physiologic porphyrinogen. A: URO-decarboxylase. B: PROTO-oxidase. C: HMB synthase deaminates PBG. D: Ferrochelatase.

questions.stem: A patient has an inherited deficiency of uroporphyrinogen III synthase. What happens to the hydroxymethylbilane she makes?

options.A: It cyclizes nonenzymatically to uroporphyrinogen I
options.B: It is decarboxylated directly to coproporphyrinogen III
options.C: It is split back into porphobilinogen
options.D: It is oxidized to protoporphyrin IX
options.E: It is excreted unchanged as ALA

questions.explanation: Without the enzyme, HMB cyclizes nonenzymatically to uroporphyrinogen I, which is converted to coproporphyrinogen I. B: Needs URO III first. C: Not shown. D: Not shown. E: Not shown.

questions.stem: Which heme synthesis intermediate is a porphyrinogen with eight carboxylate groups?
questions.explanation: Uroporphyrinogen III is an asymmetric octacarboxylate porphyrinogen; COPRO III is tetracarboxylate and PROTO IX dicarboxylate. A: Tetracarboxylate. C: Dicarboxylate. D: A porphyrin. E: A single pyrrole.

questions.stem: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase removes carboxyl groups from which side chains of uroporphyrinogen III?
questions.explanation: URO-decarboxylase removes the four carboxyl groups of the acetic acid side chains of URO III, forming the tetracarboxylate coproporphyrinogen III. A: COPRO-oxidase acts on these. B: Formed later. D: Link the rings. E: Not present.

questions.stem: Coproporphyrinogen oxidase forms protoporphyrinogen IX, a dicarboxylate porphyrinogen. What change does it make?

options.A: Turns four acetate groups into methyl groups
options.D: Turns two propionates into vinyl groups

questions.explanation: COPRO-oxidase decarboxylates two of the four propionic acid groups to form the two vinyl groups of protoporphyrinogen IX. A: URO-decarboxylase. B: PROTO-oxidase. C: Ferrochelatase. E: URO-synthase.

questions.stem: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase removes six hydrogen atoms from its substrate. What does that make its product?

options.A: The first porphyrinogen of the pathway
options.E: The first porphyrin of the pathway

questions.explanation: PROTO-oxidase forms protoporphyrin IX, a porphyrin (oxidized form), whereas the preceding tetrapyrroles are porphyrinogens (reduced forms). A: URO III is earlier. B: URO III is earlier. C: ALA is made in mitochondria. D: Heme is next.

questions.stem: An enzyme deficiency blocks a multi-step metabolic pathway. Besides a lack of product, what may cause harm?
questions.explanation: Blocks in the pathway usually lead to accumulation of precursors and lack of products, both of which may have toxic effects. A: The product falls. B: Flow is blocked. D: Substrate builds up. E: Not described.

questions.stem: Porphyrias may be inherited or arise sporadically. What do they share?

options.A: A defect in the breakdown of heme to bilirubin
options.E: Loss of one heme synthesis enzyme

questions.explanation: Porphyrias result from the deficiency of a specific enzyme in heme synthesis; they are usually autosomal dominant or recessive, but also sporadic. A: Bilirubin disorders. B: Hemoglobinopathies. C: Not the defect. D: Not the defect.

questions.stem: Porphyrias show up mainly in the tissues where the heme pathway is most active. Which are they?
questions.explanation: The enzymes are arranged sequentially in a pathway that is most active in the bone marrow and liver. B: Not the main sites. C: Where symptoms appear. D: Not the main sites. E: Not the main sites.

questions.stem: Senescent red cells are removed by the splenic sieve. About how long have they circulated?
questions.explanation: Red cells have a lifespan of 120 days; the spleen acts as a sieve that controls red cell quality. A: Far too short. B: Too short. C: Too short. E: Too long.

questions.stem: An old red cell is removed from the circulation and its hemoglobin split into heme and globin. In which cells is the heme turned into bilirubin?
questions.explanation: Heme breakdown to bilirubin occurs in the macrophages of the reticulo-endothelial system, mostly in the spleen. A: They conjugate bilirubin. C: Not the site. D: Not the site. E: They make heme.

questions.stem: Why must heme be modified before it can be excreted?

options.A: Its iron is in the ferric state
options.C: It is too large to filter

questions.explanation: The porphyrin ring is hydrophobic and must be solubilized to be excreted; bilirubin, the yellow product, is secreted in bile. A: Not the reason given. B: Not the reason given. C: Not the reason given. E: Not the reason given.

questions.stem: Where in the macrophage does heme oxygenase open the heme ring?
questions.explanation: Heme is oxidized into biliverdin, with the ring opened by heme oxygenase in the ER. A: Where heme is made. B: Not the site. C: Not the site. D: Not the site.

questions.stem: A patient with brisk hemolysis breaks down much more heme than usual. Which gas, released when heme oxygenase opens the ring, does he produce in excess?
questions.explanation: Heme oxygenase uses O2 to open the ring, releasing Fe2+ and CO and forming biliverdin. B: Not the product. C: Not the product. D: Consumed, not released. E: Released by HMB synthase.

questions.stem: A macrophage cannot supply NADPH to its heme degradation pathway. Which pigment builds up?
questions.explanation: Biliverdin reductase reduces biliverdin to bilirubin using NADPH; without NADPH biliverdin accumulates. A: Its formation needs NADPH. C: Formed in the gut. D: Formed in the gut. E: Formed in the liver.

questions.stem: Why does newly formed bilirubin travel from the spleen to the liver on albumin?

options.D: It must be oxidized on the way
options.E: Albumin carries it to the kidney

questions.explanation: Bilirubin is poorly soluble, so it is transported to the liver by albumin. A: Conjugation happens in the liver. B: Reverses the pathway. D: Not the reason. E: It goes to the liver.

questions.stem: In hepatocytes, which enzyme forms bilirubin diglucuronide?
questions.explanation: In hepatocytes bilirubin is conjugated with glucuronic acid by bilirubin UDP-glucuronyltransferase (UGT), yielding bilirubin diglucuronide. A: Forms bilirubin. C: Opens the heme ring. D: Not the conjugating enzyme here. E: Heme synthesis.

questions.stem: What does conjugation with glucuronic acid allow bilirubin to do?

options.B: Bind albumin more tightly in plasma
options.D: Travel in bile without a protein carrier
options.E: Leave the liver back into plasma

questions.explanation: Conjugation increases hydrophilicity, so bilirubin can be transported in bile without a protein carrier; unconjugated bilirubin is not normally secreted. A: Unconjugated bilirubin does that. B: Albumin carries unconjugated bilirubin. C: Not described. E: Not the purpose.

questions.stem: Which form of bilirubin is actively transported into the bile canaliculi?
questions.explanation: Conjugated (direct) bilirubin is actively transported into the bile canaliculi and then into bile to the intestine. A: Unconjugated; not secreted. B: Reduced before it leaves the macrophage. C: Formed in the gut. D: Formed in the gut.

questions.stem: A lab reports total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL (normal up to 1.2) and direct bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL. What is the calculated indirect bilirubin?
questions.explanation: Total and direct bilirubin are measured with reactive dyes; indirect bilirubin is calculated as total minus direct. B: The direct value. C: Half the total. D: The excess above normal. E: Adds instead of subtracts.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old fasting during Ramadan notices yellow eyes in exam week. Total bilirubin is 3.2 mg/dL, almost all unconjugated; hemoglobin, reticulocytes, LDH, ALT, AST and alkaline phosphatase are normal. Which enzyme is underactive?
questions.explanation: Gilbert syndrome: bilirubin UDP-glucuronyltransferase (UGT1A1) works at about 30% of normal, so bilirubin reaches the liver but leaves it unconjugated. A: Production is normal. B: Production is normal. D: Heme synthesis. E: Hemolysis is excluded.

questions.stem: A young man with yellow sclerae has a high unconjugated bilirubin, but his hemoglobin, reticulocyte count and LDH are normal. What do these normal values show?

options.D: Bilirubin is made at a normal rate

questions.explanation: Normal hemoglobin, reticulocytes and LDH mean red cells are not destroyed faster than usual: bilirubin is made at a normal rate, so the hold-up is in the liver or beyond. A: They do not measure conjugation. B: Alkaline phosphatase reflects that. C: ALT and AST reflect that. E: Not measured.

questions.stem: A man with Gilbert syndrome has a total bilirubin of 3.2 mg/dL. Why is his urine dipstick negative for bilirubin?

options.A: The renal tubules convert bilirubin to urobilin
options.E: Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin

questions.explanation: Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and poorly water-soluble, so it stays out of the urine. A: Urobilin comes from urobilinogen. B: Not the reason. C: Not the reason. D: Stercobilin is fecal.

questions.stem: A healthy 21-year-old has mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that rises with fasting and illness; liver enzymes and blood count are normal. What is the management?
questions.explanation: Gilbert syndrome is benign: no liver damage and no treatment needed, only reassurance. A: No liver damage. C: For porphyric attacks. D: For iron overload. E: No hemolysis.

questions.stem: In Gilbert syndrome, what is the residual activity of bilirubin UDP-glucuronyltransferase?
questions.explanation: Reduced activity of UGT1A1, to about 30% of normal. A: Too low. B: Too low. D: Too high. E: Too high.

questions.stem: About how many people have Gilbert syndrome?
questions.explanation: Gilbert syndrome is common: about 5 to 10% of people; mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia worse with fasting, illness and stress. B: Too rare. C: Too rare. D: Too rare. E: Too common.

questions.stem: Why may a mildly high bilirubin without liver disease benefit health?

options.C: Bilirubin protects red cells from lysis

questions.explanation: Bilirubin is a cellular antioxidant: mildly high levels in the absence of liver disease have beneficial health effects. A: Not described. B: Not described. C: Not described. D: Not described.

questions.stem: A newborn's hyperbilirubinemia climbs very high, almost all unconjugated, and he develops neurological signs. What explains them?
questions.explanation: Excessive unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood-brain barrier and accumulate in the brain: kernicterus. A: Liver failure. B: ALA and PBG. C: Lead. E: Benign.

questions.stem: Jaundice can be a sign of each of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Jaundice is usually a symptom of an underlying disorder: liver disease, obstruction or hemolytic anemia; Gilbert syndrome also causes it. A: A listed cause. B: A listed cause. D: A listed cause (hepatocellular jaundice). E: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

questions.stem: After a long course of broad-spectrum oral antibiotics, which step of bilirubin handling falls?
questions.explanation: In the intestine bacteria deconjugate bilirubin and convert it to urobilinogen; fewer bacteria means less urobilinogen. A: Hepatic. C: In plasma. D: In macrophages. E: Hepatic.

questions.stem: In the intestine, what removes glucuronic acid from bilirubin?
questions.explanation: In the intestine, glucuronic acid is removed by bacteria: bilirubin is deconjugated and then converted to urobilinogen. B: Not the agent. C: Removes glutamates from folate. D: Not the agent. E: Not the agent.

questions.stem: Where is most urobilinogen formed?
questions.explanation: Bilirubin is converted to urobilinogen mainly in the colon but also in the small intestine. A: Mostly colon. C: Bilirubin is conjugated there. D: Bilirubin is made there. E: Urobilin is made there.

questions.stem: Which pigment gives feces their typical color?
questions.explanation: Some urobilinogen is oxidized by bacterial enzymes to stercobilin, which is excreted and gives feces their typical color. A: Colors urine. B: An earlier product. C: Its precursor. E: Deconjugated in the gut.

questions.stem: Urobilinogen reabsorbed into the portal blood reaches the kidney. What does it become there?
questions.explanation: Some urobilinogen enters the portal blood, where it is recycled or goes to the kidneys and is converted to urobilin, which gives urine its color. A: Formed in the gut. B: An earlier product. D: An earlier product. E: A heme precursor.

questions.stem: A patient with blistering skin lesions has an inherited deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. Which intermediate accumulates?
questions.explanation: A block leads to accumulation of the substrate before it: URO-decarboxylase acts on uroporphyrinogen III, a porphyrinogen, and excess porphyrinogens cause skin photosensitivity. B: The product, which falls. C: A precursor further back. D: A precursor further back. E: Formed later.

questions.stem: A child with abdominal pain is being worked up for acute intermittent porphyria or lead poisoning. Which finding points to lead?
questions.explanation: Lead blocks ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in red cell precursors and causes anemia; in AIP half of HMB synthase activity suffices, so there is no anemia. A: Present in both. B: Present in both. C: Present in both. D: From PBG, which lead does not raise.

questions.stem: A man in an acute attack of intermittent porphyria is given intravenous hemin. Which enzyme is it meant to switch down?
questions.explanation: IV hemin restores heme feedback on ALAS1, cutting the flood of ALA and PBG. A: Controlled by erythropoietin and iron. C: Already half-active. D: Converts ALA to PBG. E: Breaks heme down.

questions.stem: A student has yellow sclerae. Total bilirubin is 4.0 mg/dL with direct bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL; hemoglobin, reticulocytes, ALT, AST and alkaline phosphatase are normal. Where is the problem?
questions.explanation: The raised bilirubin is almost all indirect while production is normal and the liver is uninjured: bilirubin reaches the liver but leaves it unconjugated. A: Reticulocytes and hemoglobin are normal. B: Alkaline phosphatase is normal. C: Production is normal. E: They act after bile secretion.
